title: ‘Cute’: Danish Drama Tackling Sexual Taboos Launches Trailer Ahead of San Sebastian Premiere (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 16, 2026 7:00am 'Cute' San Sebastian Film Festival The Hollywood Reporter can unveil the trailer for Marlene Emilie Lyngstad’s debut feature Cute , set to premiere at the San Sebastian Film Festival this week. The Danish film, a bold confrontation of sexual taboos, fetishisation and adult attraction to children, is written by Lyngstad and Emilie Koefoed Larse. It follows a man called Richard (Jan Gunnar Røise) who is troubled by forbidden feelings for his seven-year-old stepdaughter. He decides to leave his girlfriend and retreats to his childhood home to renovate it ahead of its sale, but his self-imposed exile is disrupted by the childlike presence of his mother’s caregiver, Stella. Related Stories Movies Why 'Sense and Sensibility' Star George MacKay Still Hasn't Watched Ang Lee's Oscar-Winning Classic Movies Avi Nesher on Bringing an Israeli Film to TIFF: "You Don't Boycott the Art" Richard soon discovers her double life as a Lolita camgirl, and the two develop a transgressive surrogate father-daughter relationship. Their constructed reality begins to unravel when the stepdaughter he left behind reaches out. The Nordisk Film Production, co-producing with Film i Väst and Amarcord, co-stars Gina Jaqueline, a social media influencer and OnlyFans creator making her feature film debut. Karin Bertling, Molly Kirk Rasmussen and Kitt Maiken Mortensen also feature. “I have accepted that I am unable to ignore the things that scare and sadden me,” said the Norwegian filmmaker Lyngstad. “This is why, through my films, I attempt to reshape apathy and melancholia into curiosity.” “Something that especially scares me is the blurred line between romantic love and fetishisation. Cute is an attempt to examine this line,” she continues. “It is a story of two people who, more than anything, long for authentic intimacy, but who can’t avoid humiliating each other in their pursuit of it.” Carl Osbæck Adelkild’s serves as producer, alongside co-producers Thomas Robsahm, Thomas Heinesen, Kristina Börjeson, Evelina Jacobsson and Johanna Bergenstråhle. Cute will premiere at the San Sebastian Film Festival on Sept. 20 in the New Directors section. The Spanish festival runs Sept. 18-26. Check out the trailer below. THR

title: Unauthorized Book on Bob Iger’s Disney Power Struggle Gets Release Date (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 16, 2026 7:00am Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan is behind 'The House of Mouse.' Courtesy of HarperCollins An upcoming and unauthorized book about Bob Iger and his tenure atop The Walt Disney Co. has Hollywood buzzing. The book, titled The House of Mouse: Bob Iger and The War of Succession at Disney , is slated for release on Dec. 1, 2026, The Hollywood Reporter has learned, with a provocative cover design featuring a Mickey Mouse-adorned crown sitting atop a red pillow (with a conspicuous bite taken out of one of the ears). Authored by Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan, THR hears that among the topics set to be covered will be Iger’s friendship-turned-rivalry with former Marvel chief Ike Perlmutter. Iger of course orchestrated the $4 billion Marvel deal in 2009, making Perlmutter one of the company’s largest shareholders. They are said to have been close, with Iger providing notes on Marvel projects and griping about compensation issues to the comic book impresario (both topics expected to be addressed in the book). Ultimately, of course, the two would be at odds, with Perlmutter helping his friend Nelson Peltz lead an activist campaign against Disney and Iger, with the billionaire being shown the door from Disney in 2023. According to the The House of Mouse’s description from publisher HarperCollins (owned by Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp., for those wondering), Whelan’s book relies “on hundreds of interviews with key figures in Iger’s orbit and thousands of pages of documentary evidence, including sensitive corporate communications and internal memos that have never been reported before.” “Whelan unspools the tale of how Iger molded Disney so tightly in his image that he became convinced that only he could run the company,” the description continues. “Iger’s reluctance to give up control led to a decade-long, Machiavellian power struggle for which Disney executives, employees, and shareholders ultimately paid dearly.” Whelan’s book concerned Disney enough that the company is said to have hired attorney Charles Harder to push for fact-checking and details on what it contains, with speculation about who some of Whelan’s sources may be, according to Puck. “At its heart, The House of Mouse is a deeply human story about the tension between creative human endeavors and the harsh realities of running a media business in the twenty-first century, and how one man struggled—as the monarch of any great kingdom must—to balance the needs of the many constituencies who love and depend on Mickey, Minnie, and the rest of Disney’s stable of beloved stories, characters, experiences, and products,” the HarperCollins description adds. Disney, it turns out, is becoming ripe fodder for the publishing world. Former CEO Bob Chapek, who was Iger’s successor in 2020 only to be ousted two years later when Iger returned, has his own tell-all called Behind the Castle Walls , which will be released later this month. “Was he really given a fair shot or was he set up to fail? What drove his ousting and Bob Iger’s return? What happened behind the scenes at Disney during COVID, and how did those decisions impact what we see today?” Chapek’s publisher says of that book. And Iger himself is said to once again be working on another book (it would be his second after the 2019 memoir The Ride of a Lifetime ), though there is no title or release date as of yet. THR

title: ‘The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives’ Review: A Twisty Nigerian Melodrama That Could Use More Mischief
full_text: Sep 16, 2026 6:59am PT ‘The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives’ Review: A Twisty Nigerian Melodrama That Could Use More Mischief Filmmaker Daniel Oriahi crafts a spirited tale that refuses to trust its own welcome excesses. By Murtada Elfadl Plus Icon Murtada Elfadl Latest ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation 3 days ago ‘What Will I Become?’ Review: Transmasculine Lives Take Center Stage in a Poignant Portrait of Loss 4 weeks ago ‘Bouchra’ Review: Animated Memoir Explores Diasporic Queer Identity and the Fraught Bonds Between Mothers and Daughters 3 months ago See All Courtesy of TIFF One of three Nigerian films playing at this year’s Toronto Film Festival , “The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” immediately throws the audience into the central dilemma of its plotty narrative. In the first scene, post copulation, Baga Segi (Odunlade Adekola) demands that his fourth and youngest wife Bolanle (Omowunmi Dada) see someone about being infertile: It’s been a couple of years since their marriage and they remain childless. From here on, filmmaker Daniel Oriahi uses voiceover and flashbacks to reveal how Bolanle arrived at this moment. Related Stories Seth Green Says He Was Never Invited Back for the Canceled 'Buffy the Vampire Slayer' Reboot This is a melodrama of malicious secrets and manipulative lies that may lead to divorce, desertion and even death. If only it committed to its heightened register instead of trying to deliver a moral, almost biblical, lesson. The screenplay, adapted from Lola Shoneyin’s novel by Oriahi alongside Adze Ugah, Mo Abudu and Heidi Uys, has many themes on its mind — among them, suffocating patriarchy, gender-based societal hypocrisy, and women’s sexual pleasure (or lack thereof) in traditional Nigerian marriages. Popular on Variety Bolanle joins a household of three wives and their many children. First there’s Iya Segi (Iyabo Ojo), the authority in the house, to whom everyone except the patriarch must bow; the other women must seek her approval for their wants and needs. Second wife Iya Tope (Mercy Aigbe) is kinder and seems mostly concerned with the wellbeing of her daughters; the film and Aigbe’s performance present her as intellectually disabled, playing into the familiar “holy fool” trope. Meanwhile, third wife Iya Femi (Bimbo Ademoye) is the most cunning and ruthless in trying to defend her position within the household, playing up to Iya Segi’s schemes as her most willing conspirator. All three are immediately threatened when Baba Segi marries Bolanle, and together, they plot a series of incidents to diminish her position. Bolanle rises above it all, taking the moral high road every time. As the film keeps reminding us, she’s the most educated of the wives — a university graduate — which undermines the others’ naturally cunning ways. Still, their outlandish schemes provide levity, pushing “The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” into welcome comic territory. Toward the end of the film, many walls of secrets come crashing down — some inexplicably so, through unprompted confessions. Those scenes play as if the screenwriters gave up on trying to resolve the twisty plot, instead just making their characters tell all, leaving the film’s denouement much less engrossing than its setup. Like the drama, the performances are heightened. At first, the three first wives appear as a sort of Greek chorus, commenting on the actions of Bolanle’s lead character. Slowly, each of their tragic stories is revealed, giving Ojo, Aigbe and Ademoye more shades to play. But they’re at their best in non-verbal scenes, with their exaggerated facial reactions to the action unspooling around them. Particularly humorous is the way they react in almost orchestrated unison at Bolanle’s wedding. In contrast, Dada is the straight woman: That her character is more realistic makes her performance more grounded, if a tad dull. As the film centers her point of view, she’s the only character keeping no secrets from the audience. Oriahi has a solid handle on all craft aspects, though only the costumes by Yolanda Okereke are particularly distinguishable — her color stories popping in almost every scene. The first three wives are dressed in the same colors at first, while Bolanle and Baba Degi appear more in tandem, evidence of who is allying themselves with whom. As the story develops, each character’s costuming grows more singular, suggesting their isolation from the others; the outfits worn by Bolanle and Iya Tope become less garish and more subdued than those of the other two wives, signifying an anchor in reality. More than any of the other elements, these costumes play at cohesion and division amongst the characters, contributing to the film’s narrative tension. But “The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” winds up too melodramatic, even for admirers of the genre. Perhaps it could have leaned more into its comedy, but what’s most disappointing is that it undermines its own dramatic flair by ending in a place of righteous moralizing. Tragedy and punishment pile up and only those characters deemed “good” by the screenplay escape unscathed. What stays with the audience are heavy-handed moral lessons, more than an entertaining couple of hours in the cinema. ‘The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives’ Review: A Twisty Nigerian Melodrama That Could Use More Mischief Reviewed online, Sept. 9, 2026. title: Broadway’s ‘Two Strangers (Carry A Cake Across New York)’ Sets Closing Date
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Judge Judy Retiring From TV Screen After 30 Years ‘Spring Awakening’ Revival Sets Principal Cast Including ‘John Proctor Is The Villain’s Amalia Yoo Rosie O’Donnell To Join Broadway’s ‘Rocky Horror Show’ As Temporary Fill-In For Rachel Dratch View All September 16, 2026 6:55am Christiani Pitts and Sam Tutty in 'Two Strangers (Carry A Cake Across New York)' Matthew Murphy Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) , the modest, two-person musical that charmed critics last season and scored eight Tony Award nominations, will play its final performance on Sunday, November 29. At the time of its closing, Two Strangers will have played 21 previews and 428 performances at the Longacre Theatre. The First National Tour of the show will launch in Providence, RI., with an expected start date in fall of 2027. Written and composed by Jim Barne and Kit Buchan, and directed and choreographed by Tim Jackson, Two Strangers stars Sam Tutty and Christiani Pitts (both Tony noninated) as two young strangers who meet when he is visiting New York (from England) for the wedding of a father he never met. Pitts plays the bride’s sister, and in opposites attract style the two bond, sometimes reluctantly, as they carry out the wedding task described in the title. Related Stories News Rosie O'Donnell To Join Broadway's 'Rocky Horror Show' As Temporary Fill-In For Rachel Dratch News 'Chicago' Sells Out With Arrival Of Ex-Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver - Broadway Box Office While the musical received favorable reviews and solid word of mouth, it did not become a major hit at the box office. In recent weeks attendance at the show was typically on the lower end of the Broadway grosses roster: Last week, attendance was at 70% of capacity at the Longacre, with a middling gross of $519,236. Watch on Deadline The Broadway production, which opened November 20, 2025, followed engagements in Boston and London’s West End. The musical is produced on Broadway by Kevin McCollum, Tim Johanson, Glass Half Full Productions, and Jamie Wilson Productions. title: Vatican to Submit a Film for Oscar Consideration, Making Academy Awards History (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 16, 2026 6:39am PT Vatican to Submit a Film for Oscar Consideration, Making Academy Awards History (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Israeli Filmmakers Among 1,500 Names to Sign Petition Defending ‘NAZA’ Directors After Their Citizenship Is Threatened Over Gaza Doc 23 hours ago ‘Gomorrah’ Writer Maddalena Ravagli to Make Directorial Debut With Sicily-Set ‘The Place of Eternal Summer’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Javier Bardem to Be Honored by Rome Film Festival With Lifetime Achievement Award 2 days ago See All Courtesy 49GlobalMedia The Vatican is set to submit a film for Oscar consideration for the first time in the 97-year history of the Academy Awards. “Green Lava,” an inspirational Vatican-produced documentary short featuring a young Italian man named Giacomo Mattivi who lives with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, will premiere this week in Los Angeles as a preamble to being submitted for Oscar consideration in the best documentary short film category. Related Stories Seth Green Says He Was Never Invited Back for the Canceled 'Buffy the Vampire Slayer' Reboot “Green Lava” will screen Sept. 18-24 at the Lumiere Music Hall in Beverly Hills. Following its theatrical run, the production team will complete the paperwork to submit it for Oscar consideration, according to a publicist for the film. Popular on Variety The submission would mark the first time a film produced by the Vatican will be in the running for the Academy Awards. That said, the film will not specifically represent the Vatican in the race. Unlike the international feature film category, short films do not need an official submission or endorsement from a national government or a country-specific committee. “Green Lava,” which is directed by Lia Beltrami and Ali Aksu, follows Giacomo “as he faces life without his brother Mattia who has just succumbed to Duchenne,” says the film’s synopsis. “Defying societal expectations, Giacomo challenges the limitations imposed by his condition and finds strength in his community and in the natural world that surrounds him.” The 39-minute film, which is set against the breathtaking backdrop of the Dolomites, is described in promotional materials as “a poignant meditation on independence, the human spirit and the transformative power of community in the face of adversity.” “Giacomo’s story deserves to be known by everyone, and that is why we are delighted about the opportunity to include ‘Green Lava’ in the Oscar submission process,” said Paolo Ruffini, who heads the Vatican’s Dicastery for Communication — which is the office that controls the Vatican’s television, radio, online, publishing and newspaper operations — in a statement for Variety. Ruffini praised “Green Lava” for being “a story that is a celebration of life and friendship,” noting that it “teaches us the richness that the lives of people marked by illness can bear witness to and offer, as well as the vitality they can bring to the relationships around them.” Director-producer Beltrami’s company Emotions to Generate Change produced “Green Lava” in collaboration with Vatican News, Radio Vaticana and Vatican Media. “I live in the same village as Giacomo and his family,” Beltrami said in a statement. “The people who live in the Dolomites, the mountains, are very special people who care and tend to their families and their communities.” She added, “It is beautiful to see in today’s world that the community has rallied around Giacomo, they treat him automatically with kindness and inclusion. It is my hope that the world will see this film and be inspired to be like the people of the mountains.” Giacomo Mattivi in “Green Lava.” Courtesy 49GlobalMedia ‘White Lotus’ Swaps the Palais for a Castle: Season 4 Cast Laura Dern, AJ Michalka and Marissa Long Drop by Disneyland Paris Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Adds Walton Goggins and Jodie Foster to Cast Bob Iger Gets All-Star Send-Off From Robert Downey Jr., Harrison Ford and New CEO Josh D’Amaro at D23 Disney Legends Ceremony Disney Is Launching a Romantasy Series Debuting on Webtoon as Webcomics Inspired by Movies Including ‘Beauty and the Beast’ ‘Disney Dreamlight Valley’ Reveals Details on Next Expansion, Including Oogie Boogie, Lilo, Hannah Montana and More ‘Kingdom Hearts’ Anime Series Based on Video Game Set for Disney+ and Disney Channel Loading comments... title: ‘Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York)’ Sets Broadway Closing Date
full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All September 16, 2026 6:35am Christiani Pitts and Sam Tutty in 'Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York).' Matthew Murphy Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) will play its final performance Nov. 29 after one year on Broadway . The two-hander musical, about a British man enthusiastically visiting New York for the first time and connecting with a cynical New Yorker, opened at the Longacre Theatre on Nov. 20, 2025, after runs in Boston and London’s West End. Sam Tutty and Christiani Pitts have starred in the show throughout its Broadway run. The closure of the show comes as gross and attendance for the show have been trending down over the last several months, with the show recently reporting 70 percent capacity and grosses around or under $500,000. The musical was nominated for eight Tony Awards, including best musical and nods for Tutty and Pitts, but did not take home any trophies. The show was written and composed by Jim Barne and Kit Buchan, and directed and choreographed by Tony Award nominee Tim Jackson. The first national tour of the show will launch in Providence, Rhode Island in fall 2027. The musical is produced on Broadway by Kevin McCollum ( Six , Oh, Mary! ), Tim Johanson, Glass Half Full Productions, and Jamie Wilson Productions. “ Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) is an incredibly special, original piece of storytelling, and an unabashed love letter to New York City,” said the producers. “Bringing this show to Broadway was a leap of faith, and audiences met us with open arms. We’re forever grateful to Tim, Kit, Jim, and the entire creative team for their beautiful work, and to the extraordinary cast – led by Christiani & Sam – and crew, for carrying the cake every night at the Longacre. We cannot wait to tour this spectacular production across the country next year on its first national tour.” THR

title: Latin Grammy Nominations 2026: Karol G, Rosalia, Jorge Drexler, Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso Lead with 7
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All September 16, 2026 6:31am Karol G accepts the Song Of The Year award for "Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido" onstage during the 26th Annual Latin Grammy Awards at the MGM Grand Garden Arena on November 13, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. Kevin Winter/Getty Images for The Latin Recording Academy The nominations for the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards are here, and it’s a four way tie for the lead among artists as Karol G , Rosalia , Jorge Drexler and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso all earned seven. All four acts received nominations in the major three record of the year, album of the year and song of the year categories. Karol G, who made history earlier this year as the first Latina artist to headline Coachella, is up for record and song of the year with “Coleccionando Heridas,” while she’s up for album of the year with Tropicoqueta . Rosalia’s “La Perla” is up for record and song, while her lauded Lux is up for album. Related Stories Music Karol G Brings Vibrant Vibes to Los Angeles With Her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour Music Rosalía Brings Her Breathtaking and Cinematic Lux Tour to Los Angeles When including non-performing producers and songwriters, perennial hitmaker Edgar Barrera was the top nominee overall with 10. Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso, who earned 10 nominations heading into last year’s awards, are up for album of the year with Free Spirts , record of the year for “Ha Ha” and song of the year with “Hasta Jesus Tuvo Un Mal Dia. Jorge Drexler, the 16-time Latin Grammy winner, is up for album of the year with Taracá , record and sonf of the year for “¿Cómo se ama?” Outside of the top four, the rest of this year’s album of the year race includes Anitta’s Equilibrium, Silvana Estrada’s Vendrán Suaves Lluvias, Mon Laferte’s Femme Fatale , Carin Leon’s Muda , Milo J’s La Vida Era Más Corta and Rawayana’s ¿Dónde Es El After? In the record of the year race, the rest of the field is Estrada’s “Dime” Loulu Gilberto’s “O Amor Nos Encontrou, Laferte’s “Femme Fatale,” “Desde Que Te Tengo,” Milo’s “Niño” and Elena Rose’s “Alma.” For song of the year, the other nominees are “Dime,” “Femme Fatale,” Juanes and Vivir Quintana’s “Humano,” Santana and Becky G’s “Mi Gran Amor,” Zanna’s Nilo” and Milo’s “Solifican12.” Rounding out the general categories, this year’s best new artist class is made up of Delilah, Fabian, Loulu Gilberto, Arath Herce, Macario Martínez, maye, Sofia Monroy, Kendall Peña, Dora Sanches, Aria Vega and Zeca Veloso. Below the four leading artists, Estrada and Laferte both earned six nominations, while Milo J got five. “We are honored to present this year’s nominees for the 27th Annual Latin GRAMMY Awards,” Manuel Abud, CEO of The Latin Recording Academy, said in a statement on Wednesday. “These artists reflect the extraordinary diversity and constant evolution of Latin music, and our Academy continues to evolve in response to this dynamic, creative landscape. At the heart of our Awards Process are our members, whose participation and expertise ensure that the Latin GRAMMY remains the benchmark for excellence in Latin music.” With the nominees announced, voting will begin on October 1. The awards themselves will take place at the MGM Garden Grand Garden Arena on November 12, airing on Univision. THR

Sheindlin – Judge Judy to millions – announced this morning that she is retiring “from in front of the camera” after 30 years of passing judgements that were often caustic, usually funny and always final. Appearing on ABC’s Good Morning America today with her son Adam Levy, lawyer and now presiding judge of TV’s new Adam’s Law show, Sheindlin said she is stepping away from her own show to focus on behind-the-scenes work including her position as executive producer of her son’s program. “I’m retiring from in front of the camera,” Sheindlin said. title: Korean Director Na Hong-jin on the Meaning Behind ‘Hope’ and His Sequel Plans: “Don’t Be Surprised If He Crosses Over to the North”
full_text: × Skip to main content Hwang Jung-min and Hoyeon in 'Hope' Neon It’s an irresistible film-nerd conceit: What would such-and-such franchise movie look like if it were directed by an arthouse auteur renowned for their singular, uncompromising vision? Say, for example, that Lars von Trier took the helm of the next Avengers movie, David Cronenberg directed Jurassic World 5 , or Wes Anderson was inexplicably brought on board for reshoots of Fast & Furious 11 . Catnip for film-geek conversation, but rarely does a movie arrive that approximates an answer. Hope , it doesn’t feel unfair to suggest, actually sort of does. This, at last, is Avatar if it were directed by South Korean maestro Na Hong-jin — the current standard-bearer for his country’s rich tradition of wildly entertaining genre cinema suffused with a sicko, trauma-tinged streak. Related Stories Movies Oscars: Spain Picks 'La Bola Negra' for Best International Feature Film Race TV 'Pride and Prejudice' Premiere Date Set at Netflix, Full Cast Photos Unveiled The 52-year-old writer-director is beloved by both arthouse fans and action aficionados thanks to a trio of unforgettable genre vehicles: the relentlessly brutal crime thrillers The Chaser (2008) and The Yellow Sea (2010), and the supernatural horror sensation The Wailing (2016). Hope , which landed in North American cinemas on Sept. 9 courtesy of Neon , shares many elements with those earlier works: characters who are lovably earthy one moment and gleefully grotesque the next, relentlessly kinetic action sequences, Na’s signature vice-grip over pacing and tone, and an above-average deployment of profanity (“ssibal,” the Korean word for “fuck,” is shouted 137 times in the film, according to a fan count widely circulated online). But it also boasts a soaring, multi-film story involving humanity’s first, hubristic brush with an enlightened race of blue-green aliens, creatures created via motion capture and lavish CGI. It’s by far Na’s most multiplex-friendly movie, but it also refuses to conform to standard tentpole storytelling conventions. Unsurprisingly, this cocktail has proved divisive. Hope premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May, drawing a six-minute standing ovation but a sharply divided critical reaction. Some, such as The Hollywood Reporter ‘s lead critic, hailed Hope as a “rip-roaring sci-fi creature feature” that “has instant cult classic written all over it.” Others — and there were more than a few — bemoaned the story’s 160-minute runtime and CGI work that betrayed a budget stretched a bit beyond its max. Set in the fictional border town of Hope Harbor near the Korean Demilitarized Zone, Hope follows put-upon police chief Bum-seok (the versatile Korean action star Hwang Jung-min) and his bad-ass female deputy Sung-ae ( Squid Game ’s Hoyeon) as they frantically hunt an enormous mystery creature that has begun rampaging through their village. A band of local hunters, led by the charismatic Sung-ki (Zo In-sung), soon join the chase and track the beast into a nearby forest. There, the discovery of a spacecraft and additional extraterrestrials transforms their chase into a simple struggle for survival, as what began as a series of understandable misjudgments spirals into a tragedy of cosmic scale. Na conceived Hope as the first chapter of a potential franchise. The film earned a healthy $36 million at home in South Korea over the summer, and brought in just over $5 million during its first extended weekend in North America. Rollouts in other markets around the world are now underway. THR recently sat down with Na at his office in Seoul to discuss his unconventional creative process, the timely message he embedded at the heart of the action spectacle, and where he plans to take the Hope saga in part two. Let’s start by talking about the creative origins of Hope . How did you get started on this story? Well, I don’t hang out with other filmmakers or people in the industry much. What I like to do is go to places that are unfamiliar to me, to meet new people, and then try things with them that I’ve never done before. In other words, I try to seek out new worlds to enter. As I’m trying to adapt to that kind of unfamiliarity, that’s where the stories I want to tell naturally come about. My films have all come from the things I learn and feel when I’m getting to know new people in totally unfamiliar situations. How did this film emerge from that process? Well, where ideas come from is always complex. But you may remember the character of Yang-bae from Hope ? (Yang-bae, played by Eum Moon-suk, is a dimwitted carpenter and taxidermy enthusiast whose clueless, greedy actions, we learn midway through the story, are responsible for setting the movie’s conflict in motion.) He’s named after a real guy I met. I have a house in Sokcho, which is a mid-sized fishing town on the east coast of Korea. I go there when I want to hide away and write. Usually, I keep to myself, but I met this guy, Yang-bae, around town. He was crazy about fishing and invited me to go fishing with him and his friends. We ended up spending a lot of time together and became quite close, going out eating and drinking. Yang-bae is the kind of person most people would call a lowlife. I would never end up spending time with a group like his in Seoul. But I learned a lot from him and his friends. He would do slimy things — like sometimes he would bring a bunch of brand-new fishing gear to sell to the group. It was unclear where or how he got it, but he was definitely selling it to his friends for a profit. Other times, he’d get everyone to pitch in on something, or split a bill, and I was certain he was taking a hefty margin. But at the same time, he was kind of the heart of the group. So I found myself observing him and thinking, is this a good or bad man? And there wasn’t really a simple answer. So, it wasn’t exactly a straight line, but I got this idea that I wanted to make a very entertaining action movie related to the notion that our biggest human conflicts usually have very little to do with whether the individuals are good or bad people. Conflicts and tragedies are almost always the result of carelessness or accidents that spiral totally out of control. And once it becomes “us versus them,” your perspective is trapped on one side or the other. I wanted to make an action movie that gives you a three-dimensional point of view on this very human problem. Did your fisherman buddies know who you are and what you do? No, they have no idea who I am. Honestly, it didn’t even really come up. They probably just thought I was another jobless bum. I definitely would never tell those guys where my house is — that would be asking for trouble. (Laughs) I consider them friends, though. Hwang Jung-min in Hope . Neon Okay, so you had this loose theme for an entertaining action film. How did you get from there to aliens? I wanted to tell a story that was as simple as possible, and in order to do that, I needed a very stark contrast. I wanted it to be about people who live in a very small village, who have a strong sense of unity and solidarity. And I wanted a very stark contrast between them and the “others” who invade their world — and eventually, the natural thought was actual aliens. The us-versus-them problem is a deeply human flaw — it’s a failing of human nature that we should be constantly aware of — so it was advantageous to have a completely other species to bring it into focus. I thought it would be fun to explore the notion that these creatures whom the humans are haplessly attacking are actually extremely noble beings from an unfathomable world. I wanted to create an almost fairy-tale structure, even though we start by filming from a human-eye view. A lot of international viewers will probably wonder whether the film is a loose allegory about the divided Korean Peninsula. I suspected that your intentions might be broader than that, though. Yeah, sure, you can view it with that interpretation. But the film’s structure, or message, could be applied to pretty much any societal conflict. The main reason I initially set the film near the demilitarized zone was more practical. [South Korea] is a very small country. If you want to tell a story in a truly remote, isolated place, that’s very hard to find here. But I needed a setting like that for the plot and action to work, and you have to go near the DMZ to find that much open space. As I was developing the story, it got longer, and I realized I would need at least a sequel, or maybe three films, to tell the whole thing. The first film takes place entirely in the daylight, but the sun is setting as we get to the end, right? Well, this is a bit of a preview, but when night comes in part two, military backup is going to arrive. Our main character, Bum-seok, he’s limping quite badly, but he’s still alive and in the fight, right? Don’t be surprised if he crosses over to the North… Oh wow, we need to see this! So, one of the things I found most impressive about Hope was how you introduce the film’s narrative complexity right in the middle of the action sequences. In any traditional chase scene, a clear understanding of hero and villain propels the action forward. But in this film, you’re constantly blurring those lines right in the midst of the melee. I can’t recall watching such visceral chase sequences where I’m simultaneously starting to question who I’m even rooting for. How did you pull this off? That was exactly the goal. Everything was really designed with that goal in mind. Without it, the chases wouldn’t need to be so long. I could have explored this through the dialog or other means, but to show that tragic dynamic via the violence and the way the two sides actually fight — it just felt more suitable, somehow. In the last chase, for example, you see this alien coming after the humans, and he’s relentless, but he’s also exhausted. In that dynamic scene, I wanted the audience to say to themselves, that’s a scary being and it’s obviously the antagonist, but why do I feel kind of sorry for him? Why does part of me want him to catch them? In a related way, once I came to understand the alien characters more by the end, it started to feel like we’ve actually been viewing the humans somewhat from their point of view all along. There’s obvious affection for the villagers’ earthy simplicity, but also a palpable sense of disgust — in the way they eat and conduct their various business. That’s exactly right. You know, when you think about it, human beings — we eat, we conduct a series of either meaningful or meaningless actions, and then we defecate. We like to think that we are part of high-minded, solidarity-driven organizations — whether nations or smaller structures — but I wanted to explore the fact that we are rarely noble. We are not superior to any other kind of being. We’re just not. These moments get interpreted as humor, but for me, it’s more like I’m poking fun, or even ridiculing, humanity. Hope has proved surprisingly divisive. At the Cannes Film Festival — a crowd of critics and hardcore cinephiles — the response was sharply divided, which is very rare these days. Some saw it as an instant cult classic; others felt it was overlong and that the VFX were undercooked. I understand it was similarly divisive in Korea. How do you account for this? Well, I think it’s pretty simple: We just didn’t have enough time and money. We knew the odds were against us. This is the first time a Korean production has attempted a spectacle of this scale. Audiences everywhere are accustomed to Hollywood blockbusters, and there’s a huge gap between the resources those filmmakers have at their disposal and what we can pull together in Korea. I can say that this was a hugely challenging feat, and we did our absolute best. For me, the quality we pulled off is high enough for audiences to fully feel and understand the film as I intended. But I understand that might not be the case for everyone. We really came up against the technical and financial limits of what’s possible in Korea. Hope Neon Tell me about working with your cinematographer, Hong Kyung-pyo (the celebrated DP behind Save the Green Planet! , The Wailing , Parasite , Burning, and more). I know he’s regarded as something of a legend in the Korean industry, and there is so much stunning camerawork in this film — the beautiful natural light; that incredibly cool effect when a car whips around a corner and the camera slingshots away from it. Before I met Hong Kyung-pyo, I always thought that one day I would also do my own cinematography. When I met him, I dropped that idea right away. I think he’s a complete genius. He’s very animalistic and instinctive, and when it comes to positioning the camera, everything just comes naturally to him. And as you said, in terms of capturing natural light, I think he has no competition. He is an absolute beast. When he proposed a wide lens with near 360-degree panning, we all said yes and wanted to cooperate immediately. That would mean finding a place to conceal our crew of 300 people — not an easy feat in these locations! — but we all gladly accepted the challenge because of how much respect we have for him, and because we knew the results would be worth it. Disaster films often tap into generational anxieties. Obviously, people are feeling pretty ill at ease, lately. No matter where you’re from, there’s a sense in the air that the world may be tipping towards truly dark times. Do you think Hope , with all the irony of that title, was born of this anxiety? Of course. I started writing Hope in 2018, around the time of the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. You might not remember, but some U.S. aircraft flew unusually close to Pyongyang and Trump was threatening a full-scale attack. There was a lot of concern and speculation about the possibility of imminent war on the Korean Peninsula — similar to what ended up unfolding in Iran. Tensions and anxiety here were really heightened. So, I do believe those events may have led to the creation of this story. And look what has happened around the world since. Every one of these ongoing conflicts is a tragedy— and every one of them is a total human folly. Did any of this violence need to go this far? Of course not. My film is a piece of entertainment, but it’s also a story that asks the question: Where should we look to, or how can we live so that humanity’s pitiful cycles of violence will finally stop? Naturally, that makes me very curious about where the story is headed in part two. I don’t expect you to tell me how you plan to end the franchise, but how confident are you that you’ll be able to finish it? Well, two entities have told me that they think the sequel has to be made and that they’re willing to finance it. Having said that, nothing is concrete just yet. But the talks so far are very encouraging. The question I’m asking myself is whether the sequel should be my next project, or if I should do something else in between. Because when I was shooting Hope , I was already birthing the idea for a new film that’s very dark — a story filled with the stench of blood. Making Hope took a long time, and I started thinking that I’ve been standing in the sunlight a little too long. The whole Hope story is about goodness, and I can feel the darkness calling to me. We’ll see what happens. THR

title: Upcoming Canadian Animated Series Shine At Cartoon Forum 2026
full_text: Sep 16, 2026 6:19am PT Upcoming Canadian Animated Series Shine At Cartoon Forum 2026 From stop-motion doggies to globe-trotting eco-conscious teens, Canadian producers captivated animation industry professionals gathered at the major European co-production event By Kevin Giraud Plus Icon Kevin Giraud Latest Heartfelt, Rare Animated Belgian Feature ‘Juul’ Headlines Studio 100 Film’s Expanding Slate at TIFF Market 2 days ago Underwater Life Breaks New Comedy Ground in ‘Submarine Jim,’ Xilam’s Latest Animated IP 6 days ago Magic Meets Mystery-Solving Trio in Mediawan’s Latest Hit, ‘Witch Detectives’ 6 days ago See All From left to right: 'Miss Tzatzikis' Classrom Mysteries,' 'Algorythm,' 'Alien Book Club', 'Labradoodles,' 'Semanka,' 'El Kapoutchi,' Courtesy of Cartoon Forum Less than two months after part stealing the spotlight in Annecy , Canadian producers, broadcasters, investors and institutional execs crossed the Atlantic once more to showcase the wide range of talents the Quebec-Canada animation industry has to offer. At the 37th edition of Cartoon Forum , Europe’s main co-production event for animated TV series once again hosted in France’s beautiful southern sunlit city of Toulouse, government funding agencies Telefilm Canada and Quebec’s SODEC , along with the Canada Media Fund (CMF) brought for the first time ever a carefully curated selection of six Quebec-Canada projects to the forefront, offering a unique platform for visibility, exchange, and co-production opportunities within the European animation industry. Related Stories Seth Green Says He Was Never Invited Back for the Canceled 'Buffy the Vampire Slayer' Reboot With projects returning from Annecy and brand-new pitches presented for the first time to a panel of worldwide investors, this dedicated session of six pitches is designed to connect creators, producers, broadcasters around the diversity of Quebec-Canada animation, opening new pathways for collaboration in an ever-more contracting global market. Popular on Variety Around this dedicated pitching session, Variety spoke with the teams of this rich, diverse panel of animated series in the making. Algorythm Producer: Extérieur Jour (Quebec-Canada) Co-producer(s): Couleur.tv (Quebec-Canada), Zeilt Production (Luxemburg) Director: Francis Gélinas Format: 26 x 5 minutes Technique: 2D, 3D Computer & Cut-out Algorythm is the name of Yasmina’s “YourTube” channel. As the most sparkling vlogger in the entire metaverse, she uses her virtual reality headset to infiltrate the Internet and talk about digital literacy. “But our protagonist Yas is not a teacher lecturing kids,” adds Elodie Pollet, producer at Extérieur Jour. “She’s one of them, and while figuring out in real time how to adapt, and build critical thinking about how children aged 9 to 13 use the internet and social media, she dives deep into digital literacy topics that are very relevant today.” Already presented in Annecy back in 2024, “Algorythm” is now in advanced development, with a teaser and a pilot episode completed in both English and French, shares Pollet. “At Cartoon Forum, we’re specifically looking to connect with an English-Canadian broadcaster, international broadcasters, and a sales agent to handle international distribution.” At this stage, Canadian broadcasters Radio-Canada and TFO have already boarded the project, and Quebec actress Mélissa Bédard is confirmed as lead voice cast. Alien Book Club Producers: Big Bad Boo Studios (Canada), Beakus (UK) Director: Shabnam Rezaei Format: 39 x 7 minutes Technique: 2D Computer Pitching for the very first time her project, director-producer Shabnam Rezaei brings “Alien Book Club” to Cartoon Forum. In her brand new upper-preschool TV series, five extraordinary aliens jump into classic stories to learn something about themselves in a huge space-age library. Because in the Intergalatic Library Bus, there’s a book and a story for everyone. “Preschoolers first fall in love with characters on the screen,” explains Rezaei, “then they imitate them. Austen, Shirl, Rumi, and the rest of our giggly aliens love to read and so with ‘Alien Book Club,’ we hope to turn our viewers into proud readers, as they become cool members of a very important club. “ It’s that premise that also appealed to Steve Smith, producer at Beakus. “Our project is a joyful celebration of books that helps children around the world fall in love with reading, with plenty of silliness along the way. With human-made animation, crafted with real care for global audiences of young readers.” At Cartoon Forum, the team is looking for co-production partners, broadcasters, streaming platforms, and investors, with CMF development backup and early interest from several public U.S. broadcasters. El Kapoutchi, the King of Villains Producer: Punch! Animation (Quebec – Canada) Director: Sylvain Lavoie Format: 26 x 7 minutes Technique: Cut-out In the town of Harmony, people share common qualities such as kindness, honesty or a sense of happiness… and El Kapoutchi hates it! A passionate and eccentric inventor, he uses his bubbling imagination to bring trouble to the quiet, peaceful town. And in his endeavor, he faces kids, who, unfortunately for him, aren’t as naive as their parents. Often craftier than the ultimate villain, they use their creativity and resourcefulness to trick him into falling victim to his own traps. An adaptation of the CBC/Radio Canada eponymous podcast by Alexandre Courteau and Pascale Richard, “El Kapoutchi” is brought to Cartoon Forum by Benoit Godbout, Sylvain Lavoie and Julie Mongeau, the trio behind Punch! Animation, who each bring their own expertise to the joint project and the company. Miss Tzatziki’s Classroom Mysteries Producer: Happy Camper Média (Quebec Canada) Director: TBC Format: 26 x 11 minutes Technique: 2D Computer In Miss Tzatziki’s Class Mysteries, everyday school life turns into thrilling cases, as four quick witted-friends try to solve the baffling mysteries of stolen sandwiches, a missing hamster, a suspicious fire alarm, and more. Blending humor, suspense and school-life situations, each episode of “Miss Tzatziki” (adapted from Patrick Doyon and André Marois’ graphic novel “The Sandwich Thief”) invites young viewers to step into the investigation, solving the case alongside the characters. “The show playfully brings the conventions of classic crime fiction into stories inspired by children’s everyday lives,” explain producers Solen Labie Trépanier and Renaud Sylvain. “Drawing on more than 15 years of the creator’s encounters with students in schools, the series turns everyday school mysteries into full-fledged investigations. The result is a funny, familiar, and distinctive world, built around universal storytelling codes that can engage both children and adults.” Radio-Canada commissioned the series, which makes its pitching debut here at Cartoon Forum. The teams are looking for broadcasters, co-production partners as well as international distribution for the series. Semanka Producer: Chrystelle Maechler Productions (Canada) Creator/Director : Chrystelle Maechler Format: 13x 11 minutes Technique: 3D Computer Returning after a successful broadcaster (TFO) / producer pitch in Annecy , “Semanka” is now building up around its IP, with CMF grants to develop a video game concept, while Maechler also received funding to develop the first draft of a book centered around these characters. “Both of these fundings send a strong signal of the franchise potential of a world that extends well beyond the screen,” adds the producer/creator of “Semanka.” “This story was born from my own mixed-race and globe-spanning family, spread across Canada, Madagascar, France, Germany, and Australia,” she continues. “Moreover, it was born out of love for my nephews, so entertainment comes first, but woven into the adventure are things I care deeply about: family ties, that sense of belonging that exists beyond distance, whether geographical or emotional.” Diversity is also a major theme in “Semanka,” a show crafted to encourage kids to build their own confidence and learn to love what might seem like quirks in themselves and others. And through its narrative, Maechler also underlines the need for protecting our nature. “Saving plants and seeds has never felt more urgent, with rising temperatures and conflicts reshaping our world. But those messages don’t need to be heavy. We trust kids’ intelligence and let them draw their own meaning from this adventure, with laughter and lightness.” Attending Cartoon Forum from end to end, Maechler seeks the right European partners (co-producers, studios, broadcasters, streamers, distributors, sales agents) to help bring “Semanka” to life worldwide, on screen and beyond. The Labradoodles Producer: Imagine Create Media (Canada) Director: Tara Hungerford, Eric Hogan Format: 10 x 22 minutes Technique: Stop-motion “The Labradoodles,” one of the few stop-motion series presented at Cartoon Forum, tells the tale of a loving family caught in the whirlwind of everyday modern life. Roger and Kate, a slowly drifting apart couple juggle work while their children Emma and Jack race between school, sports and screens. Then Roger inherits a tiny cottage on a remote island. When a storm strands the family with no wi-fi and no way home, everything changes. Forced to trade screen time for campfires, skyscrapers for forests, and schedules for sunsets, they slowly rediscover the joy of slowing down and being together. “‘The Labradoodles’ is about a modern dog family living a fast-paced city life,” explains Hogan. “Like many families today, they’re so busy keeping up that they don’t realize how disconnected they’ve become.” “We wanted to make a warm, funny, cozy family series that uses the tactile charm of stop-motion animation,” adds Hungerford, who co-directs, co-produces with Hogan and Imagine Create Media third producer Tracey Mack. “Our show explores what happens when a busy family is suddenly forced to slow down.” Imagine Create Media boasts a strong track record partnering with Canadian broadcasters and comes ready to use Cartoon Forum numerous opportunities to begin building international financing and distribution partnerships for the series. “We’re looking to meet broadcasters, distributors, co-production partners and other international partners who connect with this preschool-bridge age series with family co-viewing appeal,” concludes the team. “And we’re particularly interested in relationships that can help us build The Labradoodles into an internationally resonant, long-running pre-school property.” Thanks to the support of Canadian agencies, these teams might very well achieve this goal, reinforcing the transatlantic collaborations between European and Canadian animation industries. ‘V/H/S/MIXTAPE’ Set at Shudder; Ninth Chapter of Horror Anthology Features RZA, Ernest Dickerson, Flying Lotus and More (EXCLUSIVE) Shudder Nabs U.S. Rights to ‘Bloody Tennis’ and Horror Film Grabs Buyers in Other Major Territories Ahead of Locarno World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: ‘Julián’ Review: A Mermaid-Loving Dominican American Boy Finds Acceptance in a Vibrant Animated Delight
full_text: Sep 16, 2026 6:17am PT ‘Julián’ Review: A Mermaid-Loving Dominican American Boy Finds Acceptance in a Vibrant Animated Delight Cartoon Saloon, the Irish studio behind Oscar-nominated gems like 'Wolfwalkers,' adapts Jessica Love’s acclaimed children’s book about an imaginative boy with an immigrant grandmother trying to understand him. By Carlos Aguilar Plus Icon Carlos Aguilar Latest ‘Julián’ Review: A Mermaid-Loving Dominican American Boy Finds Acceptance in a Vibrant Animated Delight 31 minutes ago ‘The Idiot(s)’ Review: Dostoevsky Is an Endearing Drunken Fool in This Rambunctious, Tonally Off-Kilter Two-Hander 2 weeks ago ‘Camp’ Review: Guilt Is the Villain in a Transfixing, Grief-Stricken Tale of Sisterhood and Witchcraft 2 months ago See All The wondrous paintbrush of Cartoon Saloon has now reached the Latino community of Brooklyn. The acclaimed Irish studio gained international prominence (and multiple Oscar nominations) with local folktales in gorgeous animated form (“The Secret of Kells,” “Song of the Sea,” “Wolfwalkers”), and tackled an Afghanistan-set story in 2017’s “The Breadwinner.” Now, they’re once again pushing the geographical boundaries of their storytelling with “Julián,” a vibrant adaptation of Jessica Love’s acclaimed 2018 children’s book “Julián is a Mermaid.” Related Stories Seth Green Says He Was Never Invited Back for the Canceled 'Buffy the Vampire Slayer' Reboot Sea creatures materialize around seven-year-old Julián (voiced by Knyght Darius Jac), as his imagination flows freely on the drive to meet his grandmother Carmela (Milcania Diaz-Rojas) for the first time in Brooklyn. Upon dropping him off, Julián’s father warns Carmela that the boy is different, appealing to some leniency. Though neither the book nor the film makes a concrete assumption about the young protagonist’s identity, it’s clear that his gender expression is still unburdened by society’s inflexible expectations of masculinity. No prejudices against colorful clothing or jewelry have been implanted in him. Popular on Variety Vivacious and prone to daydreaming, Julián experiences a culture shock under Carmela’s roof — there’s impressive attention to detail in the production design inside her home, down to the magnets on her refrigerator. He’s not used to Dominican food or to having restrictions on what he can play with. Carmela, an immigrant from the Dominican Republic who still yearns for the people and the warm waters of her homeland, is presented as a matriarch with a firm hand, but she also genuinely tries to engage with Julián’s unique interest in the ocean and, later, with mermaids. He befriends a group of neighborhood girls who tell him about the Coney Island Mermaid Parade. He will, of course, need a costume. The character design in “Julían” differs from the subdued and elegantly playful illustrations in Love’s book, with the film leaning more cartoonish and boasting brighter, more saturated colors. What the animation brings to life is the fluid movement of water in Julián fantastical visions. The aquatic theme, the creatures Julían conjures up, and especially a sentient, fish-like sphere that the boy plays with all call to mind Hayao Miyazaki’s “Ponyo.” Furthermore, just like in that fish-out-of-water tale, a goddess of the sea makes a notable appearance. In “Julián,” it’s the Orisha deity Yemayá, whom the kid learns about through a kindhearted bodega owner, who also displays a warm and welcoming take on manhood. Though the film is directed by Irish animator Louise Bagnall — an Oscar nominee for the 2019 short “Late Afternoon,” here making her debut feature — with Guillaume Lorin and Mark Mullery as co-directors, Cartoon Saloon has made a few creative decisions to ensure cultural authenticity. The casting of Diaz-Rojas as Carmela, for example, gives the character a strongly defined personality, her nuanced voice performance shifting seamlessly between English and Spanish. The actress conveys that Carmela is a woman who has built a life in New York City over several decades, while remaining tethered to her Dominican background. More importantly, Cartoon Saloon tapped writer Juliany Taveras to pen the screenplay. Taveras — who identifies as a non-binary, queer, Afro/Indigenous Dominican American New Yorker — is the ideal artist to tackle the specific intersections of “Julián” from a place of personal, first-hand understanding of the identities that the story addresses. That Carmela mostly keeps her frustration in check, never punishing Julián for his innocent mischief, speaks to how the film challenges stereotypes around Latino households. She’s not the abuela in Pixar’s “Coco,” who imposes her trauma on her grandchild; instead Carmela listens to Julián, willing to compromise. That’s not say that “Julián” lacks conflict, because the child’s unbound flamboyance chafes against other people’s views on he should behave, through no fault of his own. His colorful mermaid costume catches the eyes of Carmela’s gossipy friends, as well as negative attention from other boys. The acceptance he eventually finds, after refusing to dim himself for being “too much,” reads more like a much-needed lesson for the adults around him than for Julián. His feat is to not let them change him. Rather, his identity grows and expands, with a newfound connection to his Dominican heritage. Thorny realities deftly observed from the perspective of young characters are present in all of Cartoon Saloon’s features so far. Even without the epic scale of some of the studio’s other works, “Julián” is a delight — elevating its urban context with visual whimsy and a focus on the intergenerational relationship at its center, more than on otherworldly magic. ‘Julián’ Review: A Mermaid-Loving Dominican American Boy Finds Acceptance in a Vibrant Animated Delight Reviewed online, Sept. 11, 2026. title: Jalen Brunson Gets Into the Brand Management Business With New Family Venture
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 16, 2026 5:58am Jalen Brunson Photo by Joy Malone/Getty Images Jalen Brunson is getting into the management business. The New York Knicks star is launching a new firm with members of his family that will manage his off-court business while also representing other clients from the world of sports and business. The new venture is called Thirty Third Management (in honor of Brunson’s pick in the 2018 NBA draft), with Brunson’s mother Sandra Brunson serving as its president and his sister Erica Brunson working as its director of client services. Brunson’s high school teammate and friend Connor Cashaw will be director of business development. While Thirty Third will obviously have Brunson as its core client, the company plans to move aggressively to represent professional and amateur athletes (taking advantage of NIL rules), as well as corporate executives, entrepreneurs, and charitable foundations, helping them on brand partnerships and development, partnerships, philanthropy and other areas. Notably the company says that it plans to make women’s pro sports an initial priority, with Erica Brunson leading that effort. Athletes have increasingly been pushing beyond the field and the court, taking advantage of their fame and recognition to launch new business ventures. Many are launching studios or production companies , seeking to carve out a piece of the media and entertainment ecosystem, but Brunson’s effort underscores how there is also an opportunity behind the scenes to help athletes and others manage their brands. “My family has been with me every step of the way, and everything we do is rooted in trust,” said Jalen Brunson. “Thirty Third gives us the chance to take ownership of my off-court business, to build something that reflects who we are, and to do it together.” “This firm was born from a belief that the most powerful brands are built on trust, purpose, and genuine human connection. As a family, we’ve had the privilege of supporting Jalen’s growth beyond basketball, and that experience inspired us to create an advisory platform that helps others do the same,” added Erica Brunson. “We are committed to helping our clients maximize opportunities, whether in professional sports, business, or philanthropy, and want to be a strategic partner that champions both success and significance.” THR

title: Patricio Guzmán Dies: Documentarian Who Chronicled Chile’s Turbulent Modern History Was 85
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Islamic Republic State Media Attacks Venice Prize-Winner Lelah Marzban Over Women’s Rights Speech The Coven Boards French Legalized Cannibalism Horror ‘Sunnyside’ As Filming Begins Venice Winner ‘Woman Unknown’ Unveils New Deals Including France In Wake Of Golden Lion Victory View All September 16, 2026 5:34am Patricio Guzman at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015 Andreas Rentz/Getty Images Chilean documentary-maker Patricio Guzmán, whose landmark documentaries included The Battle of Chile a nd Cannes prize-winner The Cordillera of Dreams, died in Paris on September 15. He was 85. Guzmán, who was born in the Chilean capital of Santiago on August 11, 1941, has been hailed as one of Latin America’s most important non-fiction directors. His landmark works include the three-part 1975-79 The Battle of Chile: The Struggle of an Unarmed People , chronicling the final year of socialist President Salvador Allende; the 1973 coup d’état which put General Augusto Pinochet in power, and resistance in the early days of the latter’s dictatorship. Related Stories News Jeremy Thomas Dies: Legendary UK Producer Of 'The Last Emperor' & 'Crash' Was 77 News Richard O'Sullivan Dies: British Sitcom Star Known For 'Man About The House' & 'Robin's Nest' Was 82 Guzmán left Chile in the 1960s to study Official Cinema School (Escuela Oficial de Cinematografía, or EOC) in Madrid. He returned home in 1971 where Allende’s government appointed him head of documentary at state cinema company Chile Films. He was chronicling the work of the socialist government when the coup broke out. Watch on Deadline The filmmaker left the country in the wake of the coup after being arrested and detained briefly. He settled in Madrid and then Paris, only returning to Chile sporadically to film, when the political situation permitted. Guzmán’s more recent credits include a trilogy reflecting on the legacy of his country’s 40-year military dictatorship: Nostalgia for the Light (2010), The Pearl Button (2015), which won Berlin’s Silver Bear for Best Screenplay, and The Cordillera of Dreams (2019), which won the Golden Eye documentary prize at the Cannes Film Festival. For his final documentary – the 2022 work My Imaginary Country – Guzmán explored his native country’s contemporary politics and the youth-led popular protests that erupted in Chile in 2019 around democracy and social equality. This special is our way of saying thank you, on behalf of every artist, industry member and fan who found a piece of themselves in her music.” Robert Deaton serves as the project’s executive producer. Dolly gave Country Music its heart, and giving some of that heart back to her is an incredible honor,” said Deaton. “My hope is simply that we do right by her story, her music and the people who love her, so that this evening feels like the tribute my friend deserves.” “Dolly Parton’s impact extends far beyond music, said Dr. Greg Jones, President of Belmont University. “She represents creativity, generosity, entrepreneurial spirit and a commitment to lifting others up, qualities that have inspired generations and resonate deeply with Belmont’s mission. It was an honor for Belmont to partner with Dolly through the launch of Dolly U and the world premiere of her musical at the Fisher Center. Now, it is a privilege to welcome artists, friends and fans from around the world to celebrate her extraordinary life and legacy from this stage in Nashville, honoring a woman whose love for Tennessee was woven into everything she did.” In conjunction with the special, CMA and Belmont University will make a donation from proceeds to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library , continuing a legacy that gives millions of children the gift of a free book each month. In addition, Disney is supporting Imagination Library to further its mission of inspiring children to imagine their possibilities. Additional details about the special, including performers, tickets and additional partners, will be announced in the coming weeks. Unveiled today at La Rochelle Fiction Festival, HBO Max is making Rush [working title], a medical drama set in Paris following a close-knit group of mobile medical teams. They race against time and their personal battles to save lives, bringing emergency medicine to street corners, metro carriages, private homes and iconic landmarks – where every call is a crisis, every decision has consequences, and every moment is a chance for human connection. Aubrey told us in March that HBO Max was developing medical dramas in both France and Italy, with no word yet on the Italian one. “To me that’s the model to emulate: Take a genre and a set of characters audiences feel very familiar with and want in their homes every week, and overlay that with a creator who is really excited to tell a specific story authentically,” she said at Series Mania. “Then you get something special that is also popular.” HBO Max is also making Bodycam [working title] in France, a thriller/horror following two beat cops who shoot an unarmed teenager, wounding him. Both are driven by a strong creative vision, each embracing a familiar genre as a toolbox to tell unique, engaging and deeply contemporary stories.” Outside of the U.S., France is one of HBO Max’s most crucial territories and the team has been commissioning local fare for a number of years. Laurel Lee (R-FL), and in the Senate by Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) and Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-HI). Rep. Laura Friedman (D-CA) and Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) appeared on a press call on Tuesday to call for a federal film incentive, telling reporters that legislation is being drafted. title: ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Takashi Miike’s Loose Remake Is a Complete Nonstarter
full_text: Sep 16, 2026 4:57am PT ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Takashi Miike’s Loose Remake Is a Complete Nonstarter Shun Oguri and Lily James lead a hardboiled but head-scratching spiritual follow-up to much better movies. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Review: A Strained Brazilian Drama About a Mother’s Apology Tour 3 days ago ‘Up Against It’ Review: Antonio Banderas Stars in a British Family Dramedy That Ignores Its Own Conundrums 3 days ago ‘A Bit of Light’ Review: A Life-Affirming Drama About a Suicidal Iranian Doctor 5 days ago See All Neon The second re-imagining of “Bad Lieutenant” — Abel Ferrara’s 1992 neo-noir starring Harvey Keitel — Takashi Miike ’s baffling “ Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo ” borrows the broad strokes of the original, but tells its own Yakuza-centric story that never fully gets going. Its stop-start approach sees numerous characters and subplots introduced before existing ones can be resolved, or even commenced in earnest, yielding a paradoxically overstuffed sequel where little of note occurs. Related Stories Seth Green Says He Was Never Invited Back for the Canceled 'Buffy the Vampire Slayer' Reboot Written by Daisuke Tengan, this loose remake opens with a block of onscreen text that fades too quickly for the human eye, before introducing the divorced, drug-addled detective Yabuki (Shun Oguri). After dropping his kids at school and snorting coke in full view of their friends — the only moment of hilarity in an otherwise bland retelling — Yabuki is called to a violent crime scene where a diminutive Yakuza member has been tied up in a sexual rendezvous gone awry, before having his neck turned nearly all the way around. The grisly diorama doesn’t faze Yabuki, and although he’s expected to offer expert testimony given his Yakuza-chasing past, he would rather let things lie. Instead, he offers a tip about the story to a bookie to clear some of his own gambling debts before going right back to baccarat. Popular on Variety In the pockets of unsavory people (some of them Yakuza bosses), Yabuki is soon pulled into a second series of killings, this time involving a gang member released from prison hacking his way through past associates, and turning their remains into meatballs — the only image here that provokes a visceral reaction. A little digging takes Yabuki to the suspected killer’s former orphanage, where he learns a tidbit about his past, only for the film to sweep all this aside in favor of several new detours which, although semi-connected, never fully cohere. Running parallel to this butchery investigation is the arrival of perpetually hungover FBI agent Gwen Birgssen, played by British actress Lily James with an incomprehensible southern drawl and some clunky platitudes that veer into genre parody. Also beholden to major power players, Birgssen is in Japan searching for the wild-child daughter of an American politician, culinary student Megan (pro wrestler Gionna Daddio, credited by her WWE name Liv Morgan). After a chance meeting with Yabuki, she decides to enlist his help: At this point, it mercifully seems like the movie might finally kick off, only for it to stall for the umpteenth time. First-act setups extend through the majority of the 108-minute runtime, constituting a plotless meander without the aesthetic allure to justify such a languid journey. Despite being set against the sprawl of Tokyo’s nightlife, the film feels severely limited in its use of time and place, and never crafts an atmosphere worthy of Miike’s previous work — one alluring or lurid enough to counterbalance its thematic and dramatic emptiness. Apart from brief flashes Yabuki sees of a former partner he betrayed, there’s nothing really going on beneath the surface, as empty Japanese and American suits talk in circles about their opaque pasts. They don’t connect any major dots in either criminal case; both are solved by other people calling them with information. The occasional neon nightclub plays host to a skirmish here or there — the only major setpiece unfolds practically at random, completely disconnected from the plot — before Birgssen disappears for lengthy periods, leaving us to follow the passive Yabuki doing little of interest beyond borrowing money, visiting sex workers, and having repetitive interactions with low-level goons and the occasional mob boss. Where Ferrara’s original and Werner Herzog’s 2009 version (“Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans”) shoved their violent lawmen towards spiritual agony, Miike only goes as far as cornering Yabuki within the frame a few times, before hitting the reset button yet again. By the time the film takes its first intriguing turn — some 15 minutes before the credits — it loses the time and the goodwill to have it mean much, beyond a puzzling series of loosely interconnected scenes that, at best, echo an underdeveloped idea of what a Japanese “Bad Lieutenant” might look like. ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Review: Takashi Miike’s Loose Remake Is a Complete Nonstarter Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (Special Presentations), Sept. 15, 2026. Executive producers: Paula Paizes, Ivan Kelava, Peter Watson, Yuzo Kuwahara, Nobuyuki Iinuma, Tetsu Fujimura, Max Loeb, Mike Apgar, Tom Quinn, Sarah Colvin, Kristen Figeroid, Laurel Charnetsky, Alainée Kent. Crew: Director: Takashi Miike. Screenplay: Daisuke Tengan. Camera: Nobuyasu Kita. Editor: Naoichiro Sagara. Music: Koji Endo. title: Islamic Republic State Media Attacks Venice Prize-Winner Lelah Marzban Over Women’s Rights Speech
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Islamic Republic State Media Attacks Venice Prize-Winner Lelah Marzban Over Women’s Rights Speech The Coven Boards French Legalized Cannibalism Horror ‘Sunnyside’ As Filming Begins Venice Winner ‘Woman Unknown’ Unveils New Deals Including France In Wake Of Golden Lion Victory View All September 16, 2026 4:18am Laleh Marzban poses with the Orizzonti Best Actress Award for Falling House Andreas Rentz/Getty Images Laleh Marzban, who won Best Actress in Venice Film Festival’s Orizzonti sidebar, has become the subject of a harsh smear campaign by Islamic Republic state media over comments in her acceptance speech dedicating the prize to the women of Iran . One TV station channel, aligned with the Basij, the paramilitary volunteer militia within the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), accused Marzban of turning her back on Iran, while other Islamic Regime-backed channels have accused her of treason and suggested the Ministry of Culture should ban her from returning to Iran. The Iranian actress Marzban was feted for her performance in Mohsen Gharaei’s drama Falling House (Mogareb), revolving around three generations of women in an economically fragile family, living under the thumb of the prison guard father. Related Stories News Iranian Director Mohsen Gharaei Talks Navigating Censors To Bring Prophetic Drama ‘Falling House’ To Fruition – Venice News Venice Winner ‘Woman Unknown’ Unveils New Deals Including France In Wake Of Golden Lion Victory Marzban plays the lead female role of the oldest daughter who the father locks-up on discovering her plans to leave Iran to pursue dreams of becoming a model, appearing on screen both with and without a hijab. Watch on Deadline The film’s director Gharaei told Deadline prior its world premiere in Venice that he had written the first draft in 2018 but that the 2022 Woman Life Freedom protests had given him fresh impetus to get the production off the ground. Sparked by the death in police custody on September 16, 2022 of Mahsa Amini, following her arrest for not wearing her hijab correctly, the protests saw hundreds of thousands of Iranian women and men take to the streets in Iran to call for an end to the draconian Islamic Republic rules around female dress codes and conduct. At the Venice Film Festival awards ceremony on Saturday evening, a tearful Marzban acknowledged that Iran and its people were going through “the hardest days” and dedicated her award to all Iranian women. “I dedicate my award to the women of my country who have paid the highest price for the smallest freedoms,” she said. “These women today carry dreams, courage and hope, and I believe that one day the wish of all of us will come true.” Iranian actress Zhila Sadeghi, who is known for her affiliation with Republic of Iran’s state broadcaster (IRIB), attacked Marzban for not dedicating her speech rather to the children killed in a U.S. missile strike on an elementary school in Minab on the February 28. She said that Marzban had betrayed Iran, adding “curse the ones who let you have a role in a film ever again”. Marzban, whose credits include the 2023 Iranian Oscar submission The Night Guardian , has never been at odds with the Islamic Regime before. Marzban was asked by Deadline at the Venice Orizzonti winners press conference how she thought the film would be received in Iran given that it challenged the government and its patriarchal system. “This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective,’ she said. “If we give our small contribution, maybe we will reach our objective. I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.” TV Ratings, Review, Winners, Snubs & Surprises, Scorecards; More Casey Bloys Celebrates HBO’s 21 Emmy Wins, Gives Updates On 2027 Slate Trump’s DOJ Backs Company In Battle Over Antitrust Suit’s $1.88B Bond Robert De Niro In Talks To Play Tommy Lasorda In Skydance Sports’ ‘Tommy & Me’ Read More About: Comments
